title: Scaffolding a Mathematics Lesson, with Help from Artificial Intelligence
author: Harry Zafar
summary: Harry Zafar, a secondary maths teacher, shows how he uses generative AI to produce the many small scaffolding resources that would otherwise be too time-consuming to create by hand. He is clear that the thinking is not outsourced: the AI handles procedural resource creation while he decides how to break a process into parts and sequence checks for understanding. Using a worked example on finding the nth term of a linear sequence with a Year 10 class, he walks through prompts given to a Gemini Gem to generate mini-whiteboard checks, graded practice sets and answer reveals, first for increasing and then for decreasing sequences. A second example applies the same structure to factorising non-monic quadratics. The piece is a teacher-level workflow guide in which the AI tool supports an explicit-instruction approach rather than replacing it.
points: Zafar uses AI only for the procedural work of generating scaffolded questions, keeping lesson design and sequencing as the teacher's thinking.
He defines scaffolding as isolating smaller parts of a process so students understand each before combining them.
A configured Gemini Gem produces mini-whiteboard checks, graduated practice sets and click-to-reveal answers on demand.
Practice is deliberately restricted to increasing sequences first, then decreasing ones, with mixed sets held back until the scaffold is removed.
The same part-by-part structure is reused for factorising non-monic quadratics.
quotes: The thinking is not being outsourced to artificial intelligence; rather, the AI is completing the procedural parts that I find are a barrier to effectively scaffolding a lesson, due to time constraints in creating them.

I use the term scaffolding to mean providing support that enables students to focus on smaller individual parts of a process and to ensure they understand these parts before bringing them together to understand the full process.

This is a check for understanding, using mini-whiteboards. It gives me back the following, which allows me to check that students understand this idea and for them to think about it and embed it before we move on.

Once I see that all students can do this, I give them a set of questions. I again use AI for this because I want students to get lots of practice with increasing sequences before we look at decreasing sequences, and it would be difficult to find a set of 20 questions that already exist.
I again use a Gem, which ensures that questions gradually increase in difficulty and allows me to click to reveal answers as students work through them.

At this point, I would have ideally given students a mix of increasing and decreaing sequences to check that they can identify if the nth term starts with for example +3n or -3n, to further take away the scaffold that was given by all the questions so far either being increasing or decreasing in the same activity. However, I ran out of time, so I will do this next lesson.

This is intended to serve as an example of how AI can aid in scaffolding lessons. You may disagree with some of my choices or find improvements, but I hope you might take some ideas about how it can help support students in your classroom.
